planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and roots shaded; this integrifolia x Jackmanii hybrid lacks twining leaf-stalks, so it needs to be tied to a support or allowed to sprawl through neighboring shrubs.

directions: Plant with roots kept cool and shaded while the top growth reaches into full sun. A cross between the herbaceous C. integrifolia and the vining C. Jackmanii group, Durandii combines large, deep indigo-blue, slightly nodding flowers with cream stamens and a semi-scrambling habit that has none of the twining petioles typical of climbing clematis, so it must be woven through a support or tied loosely to wire or a low fence. It blooms in flushes from midsummer into early fall entirely on new wood, so cut the whole plant back hard in late winter. Water regularly through the growing season and mulch to keep the root run cool and moist.

common_name: Mayleen Clematis (Vigorous Bronze-Leaved Pink Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering if size control is needed (Group 1); give it a large, sturdy structure since it grows extremely fast and vigorously once established.

directions: Give this exceptionally vigorous montana cultivar a large arbor, pergola, or wall since it can cover twenty feet or more once established. In mid to late spring it produces a dense, single flush of fragrant, mid-pink flowers with golden stamens against emerging bronze-purple foliage that later greens up. Because it flowers on the previous year's wood, any pruning to control size or shape should happen immediately after the bloom period rather than in late winter. Plant where roots stay cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun, and water well the first two seasons while the extensive root system establishes.

planting.note: Prune hard in late winter (Group 3) since it flowers on new growth produced the same season; can also be planted in fall in mild climates.

directions: One of the older large-flowered cultivars still widely grown for its late, reliable display, Ascotiensis opens generous violet-blue flowers with a slightly ruffled edge and cream stamens from midsummer into early fall, well after most spring-flowering types have finished. Because it flowers on new wood, cut all stems back to a strong pair of buds about a foot above ground in late winter to keep growth vigorous and flowering low enough to enjoy. Give it a trellis, obelisk, or wires to climb, with roots shaded and cool and the top growth in full sun. Water consistently through summer, especially while the plant is establishing.

planting.note: Light prune only (Group 2); flowers on old wood in early summer, then produces single flowers on new growth later in the season.

directions: Introduced in the 1870s and still grown for its old-fashioned charm, Proteus opens fully double, rounded rosettes of mauve-pink in early summer on the previous year's wood, then follows with smaller single or semi-double flowers of the same color on new growth later in summer. This two-stage bloom habit means only light, shaping cuts should be made after the first flush rather than a hard annual cutback. Give it a trellis or wires in full sun with the base of the plant shaded and mulched, and water regularly through the growing season, particularly during the extended repeat bloom.

common_name: Louise Rowe Clematis (Double-to-Single Pale Mauve-Pink Clematis)

planting.note: Light prune only (Group 2); the earliest flowers on old wood are the most fully double, with later flushes on new growth opening single or semi-double.

directions: Louise Rowe is prized for changing form through the season: its first flush on overwintered stems in late spring is fully double, a soft pale mauve-pink rosette with a silvery sheen, while later flowers produced on new growth open as elegant single or semi-double blooms in the same soft color. Because the showiest double flowers come from old wood, prune only lightly right after the first flush to remove spent stems rather than cutting the whole plant back. Grow it on a trellis or wires with roots shaded and the top in full sun to light shade, and keep soil evenly moist through the growing season.

common_name: William Kennett Clematis (Large Lavender-Blue Red-Anthered Clematis)

planting.note: Light prune only (Group 2); flowers heavily on old wood in early summer with a lighter repeat on new growth in late summer.

directions: A Victorian-era introduction from the Jackman nursery still valued for its huge blooms, William Kennett produces some of the largest flowers of any large-flowered cultivar, pale lavender-blue with a darker central bar and conspicuous deep red-brown anthers that give strong visual contrast. The main flush comes on overwintered stems in early summer, so limit pruning after flowering to removing dead or crowded growth rather than cutting hard, and expect a lighter second flush on new wood in late summer. Plant against a trellis or wires with roots cool and shaded, and water deeply during dry spells, especially in the first two seasons.

common_name: Jackmanii Rubra Clematis (Double Red-Purple Jackman Sport)

planting.note: Prune hard in late winter (Group 3), cutting all stems back to a strong pair of buds a foot or so above ground since flowers form on new growth.

directions: A distinct sport of the classic Jackmanii, this cultivar carries the same reliable, easy-care vigor but opens richer reddish-purple, semi-double to double flowers instead of Jackmanii's single violet-purple blooms. Flowering runs from midsummer into early fall on wood produced that same season, so cut the entire plant back hard each late winter to keep it dense and floriferous rather than bare at the base. It climbs readily on a trellis, wires, or through an open shrub, and performs best with roots shaded and cool while the vine reaches into full sun. Water regularly through summer heat.

common_name: Beauty of Worcester Clematis (Double Violet-Blue Heritage Clematis)

planting.note: Light prune only (Group 2); the double flowers form on old wood, with single blooms of the same color following on new growth.

directions: Raised in England in the late 1800s and still sought after for its old-fashioned double flowers, Beauty of Worcester opens rich violet-blue rosettes with contrasting cream-white stamens on overwintered stems in early summer, followed by simpler single flowers of the same deep blue-violet on new shoots later in the season. Prune lightly after the first flush, removing only dead or crowded stems, since a hard cutback would sacrifice the prized double blooms. Grow it on a trellis or wires with the root zone shaded and mulched and the vine itself in full sun, watering regularly through dry summer stretches.

common_name: Marcel Moser Clematis (Large Striped Pink-Mauve Clematis)

planting.note: Light prune only (Group 2); the main flush is on old wood in late spring, with a lighter repeat on new growth in late summer.

directions: Bred by the Moser nursery in France in the same era that produced Nelly Moser, this cultivar carries a similar striped pattern, with pale mauve-pink petals marked by a bold carmine-pink central bar and dark red anthers. Flower color holds best when the vine is shielded from intense afternoon sun, since strong direct light can bleach the delicate bar pattern, so a partly shaded exposure or an east-facing wall suits it well. Prune lightly right after the first flush to tidy the plant, since hard cutting back would remove the wood that carries the season's best bloom. Water regularly and keep the root run cool and mulched.

common_name: Wada's Primrose Clematis (Pale Yellow Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Light prune only (Group 2); flowers mainly on old wood, with a smaller repeat flush on new growth in late summer.

directions: Named for the Japanese nurseryman who raised it, this cultivar is unusual among large-flowered clematis for its pale, creamy primrose-yellow petals, which fade toward white as the flowers age and take on a faint pink flush at the base in cool weather. Bloom is heaviest in late spring on overwintered stems, so limit pruning after flowering to removing spent or damaged growth rather than a hard cutback, which would forfeit the main display. Grow it on a trellis, obelisk, or wires with roots shaded and cool and the vine reaching into full sun, and water consistently through the growing season.

common_name: Diamond Ball Clematis (Double Lavender-Blue Pompon Clematis)

planting.note: Light prune only (Group 2); double flowers form on old wood, with single blooms following on new growth later in the season.

directions: Part of a modern Polish breeding program aimed at compact, container-friendly clematis, Diamond Ball produces tightly packed, spherical double flowers in soft lavender-blue that resemble small pompons, opening on overwintered stems in late spring and early summer. Its shorter, more restrained growth makes it well suited to a large patio pot on an obelisk as well as a small trellis in the border. Prune only lightly after the first flush to preserve the wood that carries the double blooms, and expect simpler single flowers on new growth later in summer. Keep the root zone cool and shaded and water regularly, especially in containers, which dry out faster than garden soil.

common_name: Belle of Woking Clematis (Double Silvery-Mauve Heritage Clematis)

planting.note: Light prune only (Group 2); the fully double flowers form on overwintered stems and are lost if the plant is cut hard.

directions: Raised in the English town for which it is named in the 1870s, Belle of Woking is grown today mainly for the novelty and history of its fully double, silvery lilac-mauve rosette flowers, which appear on old wood in late spring and early summer with a symmetrical, camellia-like form. Because the double flowers rely on wood carried over from the previous year, prune only lightly right after bloom to remove weak or dead stems rather than cutting the plant back hard. Provide a trellis or wires in full sun with the root area shaded and mulched, and water regularly, particularly while the plant is becoming established.

common_name: My Angel Clematis (Compact Non-Vining Deep Purple-Blue Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a compact, non-vining clematis suited to a patio container or the front of a border without any climbing support.

directions: Bred from the herbaceous, non-climbing integrifolia line, My Angel forms a small, self-supporting mound rather than a vine, bearing nodding, bell-shaped, deep purple-blue flowers with recurved petal tips over a long stretch from early summer into fall. Its compact size makes it a natural choice for edging a border or filling a large patio container, where it needs no trellis or stake. Because it blooms entirely on new growth, cut the whole plant back close to the ground in late winter to keep it tidy and encourage the strongest flush the following season. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch to protect the shallow root system from summer heat.

common_name: Innocent Blush Clematis (Compact Double Pale Pink Patio Clematis)

planting.note: Light prune only (Group 2); bred for a compact, bushy habit well suited to a large container on a small obelisk.

directions: Bred as part of a modern patio-clematis collection aimed at gardeners with limited space, Innocent Blush stays compact and bushy while still producing an abundance of fully double, pale blush-pink flowers that open on overwintered wood in mid to late spring, with a lighter repeat of simpler flowers on new growth later in the season. Its restrained size and dense habit make it well suited to a large pot on a small trellis or obelisk as well as a spot at the front of a mixed border. Prune only lightly after the main flush to keep the wood that produces the double blooms, and water container plants especially often since they dry out faster than garden soil.
